entities.summary:
John Palsgrave (died 1554) was a pivotal figure in the early Tudor English court, serving as a chaplain and tutor during the reign of King Henry VIII. His significance lies in his contributions to royal education and, more broadly, to the standardization of French language instruction in England during a period of intense cultural and political exchange between the two nations. As a humanist scholar, Palsgrave embodied the intellectual currents of the burgeoning English Renaissance, bridging practical pedagogy with scholarly linguistic pursuits, thereby influencing both courtly erudition and broader educational practices.

Educated at Cambridge and possibly Paris, Palsgrave entered royal service around 1514, becoming a tutor to Princess Mary, daughter of Henry VIII and Catherine of Aragon. His most enduring achievement is *Lesclarcissement de la Langue Françoyse* (1530), a monumental French grammar and dictionary printed by Richard Pynson. This comprehensive work, dedicated to Henry VIII, was designed to teach French to English speakers, providing detailed phonological, morphological, and syntactic explanations, alongside an extensive vocabulary. Beyond his linguistic scholarship, Palsgrave held several ecclesiastical preferments, including the rectory of Kegworth in Leicestershire, indicating his dual role within the spiritual and intellectual spheres of the Tudor establishment.
